The last lighthouse on Earth stood three hundred miles from the sea, between a laundromat and a shop that repaired umbrellas.

Its plaque claimed it had been built to guide vessels through a strait that appeared on no map. Children were told it was a water tower. Pigeons, who might have corrected them, kept their own counsel.

For thirty-one years, the keeper was a woman named Mina Vell. She had inherited the job from her father, along with 119 iron steps, a brass key the size of a spoon, and a single piece of advice: *Light it before you need it.*

So at six every evening, earlier in winter, Mina climbed the tower. She cleaned the lens, checked the lamp, and opened the seaward shutter, though the seaward side faced a bingo hall. Then the beam went out over the city: across chimneys, billboards, hospital windows, and the narrow gardens where people grew tomatoes in spite of everything.

Most citizens used it to tell time. If your laundry was still wet when the light passed, you had stayed too long at the bar. Insomniacs swore the beam made a sound, though the lamp was electric. A man on Sable Street set his clocks by it; he was always seven minutes late and completely reliable.

Every few years, an inspector from Public Works arrived.

“No coastline,” the inspector would say.

“No,” Mina would agree.

“No shipping.”

“Not that I’ve noticed.”

“No strategic purpose.”

At this, Mina usually put on the kettle. Inspectors found it difficult to condemn a building while holding a warm cup. They left their forms behind. She left the forms unsigned. It was astonishing, she thought, how long a thing could survive if everyone assumed someone else had decided it should.

Occasionally, someone knocked on the lighthouse door after midnight. Not often enough to frighten her, but often enough to justify keeping a second cup.

Once it was a girl with a suitcase and no ticket. Once, an old man in a wedding suit. Once, a nurse who had forgotten the way home after a double shift, though she had lived on the same street for twelve years.

Mina let them sit beneath the turning light. She gave them tea, or silence, whichever seemed more nourishing. She never asked where they were going. People who are truly lost often become stubborn when asked for a destination.

Usually they left before dawn. Sometimes they remembered an address. Sometimes they only remembered that they were tired, which was a beginning.

They left behind buttons, ticket stubs, a single red glove, and, on one occasion, a paper crown. Mina kept these in a drawer labeled SPARE PARTS.

Then, on a wet October night, the lamp went out.

It did so politely, with a small click.

Mina replaced the bulb. She cleaned the contacts. She struck the housing once with the flat of her hand, because her father had done this and because machines, like donkeys, occasionally responded to an old language.

Nothing.

Outside, rain needled the windows. Below, the city continued without its beacon. Buses sighed at corners. The laundromat’s dryers turned. Somewhere, a dog barked itself hoarse at absolutely nothing.

Mina sat beside the dead lamp until nearly three. Then she put on her father’s coat and went down.

At the bottom of the stairs, she stopped.

The street was full of lights.

Not many at first glance—perhaps forty, perhaps sixty—but enough to make a ragged constellation around the tower. The woman from the laundromat held a fluorescent tube plugged into an extension cord. The umbrella repairer had brought a lamp with a green shade. The nurse stood beneath a pharmacy lantern. A child held a flashlight under his chin, producing an effect he clearly regretted.

No one had organized them. That was the part Mina would think about later. One person had noticed the darkness and come outside. Another had seen that person from a window. Lights had been fetched. Coats had been put on over pajamas.

“The lamp’s broken,” Mina said.

“We know,” said the umbrella repairer. “That’s why we’re standing in the rain.”

Someone laughed. Someone else offered her a thermos. Mina took it without asking what was inside.

She had spent her whole working life behind the light. She had never considered how different the lighthouse must look from the other side: not a room, not a duty, not 119 steps climbed by aging knees, but a white tower with something burning at the top.

The lighthouse remained dark for nine days. Nothing happened to the ships, there being no ships. But each night someone left a light at the foot of the stairs.

On the tenth evening, Mina installed the new lamp. She lit it before sunset.

Then, instead of staying beside it, she went down to the street.

From there, the beam looked nothing like she had imagined. It did not command the darkness. It simply crossed it, touching a chimney, a clothesline, the white face of a clock, before going on past everything she knew.

“Where does it end?” the child with the flashlight asked.

Mina thought of her father, the drawer of buttons, and all the strangers who had slept in her chair. She thought of the years she had kept the lamp burning because she did not know what else to do with her hands.

“At somebody’s window,” she said. “Probably.”
